summary:
On long missions to the Moon or Mars, help from Earth can be minutes away, while astronauts face radiation, isolation, altered gravity and a closed environment. These hazards can cause immune changes, bone loss, cardiovascular problems and behavioral health issues, and the crew often notices them first.

VitalOrbit is a self-monitoring tool designed from the astronaut’s point of view. Astronauts log ten health indicators, and the app shows each one as green, amber or red at a glance. It flags “drift” when a value is still normal but moving the wrong way, and gives a plain-language action for every warning. An interactive body map links each part of the body to the spaceflight hazard that affects it, explains why it matters, and shows how to take the measurement. Trend charts show the last 21 days, and the app adapts its context for a space station, deep-space transit, lunar base or rover.

To keep the routine going, VitalOrbit adds daily health missions with XP, levels and streaks, plus configurable measurement reminders. When help is needed, it produces a one-click summary and data file for the flight surgeon on the ground.

It is built with React and a Python (FastAPI) backend that holds all the health rules in one place. Reference ranges are simplified for demonstration and not clinically validated; VitalOrbit is an educational prototype, not a medical device.
details:
What it does. VitalOrbit is a self-health monitor for astronauts on long missions, where help from Earth can be minutes away. The astronaut logs ten indicators: heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, blood oxygen, breathing rate, blood sugar, body temperature, sleep, mood and exercise. Each is shown as green, amber or red. The app also flags “drift” when a value is still in range but moving the wrong way over recent days. Every warning comes with a plain-language action, including when to contact the flight surgeon. A clickable body map links each body region to the spaceflight hazard that affects it (isolation, radiation, altered gravity, a closed environment, distance from Earth), explains why it matters and shows how to take the measurement. Trend charts cover the last 21 days.

Benefits and impact. Astronauts don’t need medical training to use it. It catches slow changes such as falling sleep, rising heart rate or less exercise before they become serious, and it supports crews on delayed-communication missions to the Moon and Mars. Reminders, daily health missions, XP and streaks keep the routine going. A one-click report and data file give the ground flight surgeon a clear summary.

How it works. The app adapts to four settings (space station, deep-space transit, lunar base, rover), changing the signal delay and context shown. Each indicator has a “watch” range and an “action” range. A readiness score combines the red, amber and drifting indicators.

Tools. React and Vite for the interface, Python and FastAPI for the health rules, drift detection, XP and reports, SVG for the body map, charts and icon, and GitHub Pages for hosting. The design is based on NASA’s Human Research Program hazard and risk pages and the Canadian Space Agency’s articles on radiation monitoring and astronaut health.

Creativity. It is designed from the astronaut’s own point of view instead of mission control’s, and it explains every measurement for non-experts. The body map is interactive, drift detection warns before a value goes out of range, and the game elements encourage healthy habits.

Factors considered. Reference ranges are simplified and not clinically validated, so this is an educational prototype, not a medical device. Next steps are sensor and wearable input, camera or ultrasound images, multi-crew profiles and an offline-first version for delayed communications.
